theory.intro: Different displays suit different data and purposes. Identify the data type and what you want the graph to show.
facts: **Column graphs** compare quantities for categorical or discrete numerical data. A **picture graph** uses symbols and a key, but many symbols can take a long time to draw.
**Line graphs** show change over time and allow estimates between measurements.
**Sector graphs** and **divided bar graphs** show proportions of a whole for categorical or discrete numerical data.
**Dot plots** and **stem-and-leaf plots** show the distribution of discrete numerical data, including clusters and outliers. Large frequencies can make these displays crowded.
**Histograms** and **frequency polygons** show the distribution of numerical data, including continuous measurements.
Choose an axis **scale** so the largest value fits and gaps are even (e.g. steps of $5$ or $10$).
steps: Identify whether the data are categorical, discrete numerical or continuous numerical.
Identify the purpose: compare quantities, show change over time, show proportions of a whole or show a numerical distribution.
Choose a display suited to both the data type and purpose, considering whether the amount of data makes it difficult to draw or read.

workedExamples.question_text:
A class records its favourite outdoor activities.

| Activity | Number of students |
| --- | --- |
| Cycling | 9 |
| Swimming | 12 |
| Walking | 6 |

Choose a suitable graph for comparing the numbers. Explain your choice.
workedExamples.solution_text: Use a **column graph**. The activities are categories, and separate column heights make their numbers easy to compare.

workedExamples.question_text:
A gardener records a plant's height at the end of four consecutive weeks.

| Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Height (cm) | 8 | 11 | 15 | 18 |

Choose a suitable graph for showing how the height changes over time. Explain your choice.
workedExamples.solution_text: Use a **line graph**. Place the weeks in order on the horizontal axis and height on the vertical axis. Joining consecutive measurements shows how the height changes over time.

workedExamples.question_text:
Students count birds at three named parks: Riverside $6$, Hilltop $10$ and Lakeside $8$.

A student suggests joining the three counts on a line graph. Explain why this is inappropriate for comparing the parks, and suggest a suitable graph.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The park names are categories. A line would suggest meaningful values between park names, but there is no halfway park between Riverside and Hilltop.

Use a **column graph** with a separate column for each park.

workedExamples.question_text:
A class records its favourite fruit.

| Fruit | Number of students |
| --- | --- |
| Apple | 12 |
| Banana | 6 |
| Orange | 6 |

Which is more useful for showing each fruit's share of all choices: a column graph or a sector graph? Explain your choice.
workedExamples.solution_text: Use a **sector graph**. The whole circle represents all choices, and each sector represents one fruit's share of the whole.

workedExamples.question_text:
A shop sells $150$ pencils, $230$ pens and $320$ markers in a week.

A proposed picture graph uses one carefully drawn picture for every item sold. Explain why a column graph would be more appropriate for comparing these sales.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The picture graph would require hundreds of drawings, making it slow to draw and read.

A **column graph** compares the sales using three columns. An even vertical scale in steps of $50$, from $0$ to $350$, would fit the largest count.

workedExamples.question_text:
A library records how many books each visitor borrows.

| Books borrowed | Number of visitors |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 120 |
| 2 | 180 |
| 3 | 260 |

Would a dot plot with one dot per visitor be a practical display? Explain your answer.
workedExamples.solution_text:
No. Although the numbers of books are numerical counts, the frequencies would require hundreds of dots. The dot plot would be crowded and slow to draw and read.

A **column graph** could show the three book counts and their frequencies more clearly.

foundation.question_text:
A nature group counts sightings by animal: wallaby $12$, kookaburra $8$, possum $5$.
Choose a suitable display.
foundation.solution_text: The data compare categories, so use a **column graph**.

foundation.question_text:
Water temperature at a creek is recorded each day for one week.
Choose a suitable display.
foundation.solution_text: The data show change over time, so use a **line graph**.

foundation.question_text:
A junior ranger records frog sightings at three ponds: Banksia $5$, Creek $7$ and Meadow $9$.
Explain why a line graph is not appropriate for comparing these counts.
foundation.solution_text: The ponds are categories. Joining their counts suggests meaningful values between pond names, so a line graph is not appropriate.

foundation.question_text:
A bird survey records sightings by habitat. The ranger wants to show each habitat's share of all sightings.
Which is more useful: a column graph or a sector graph?
foundation.solution_text: Use a **sector graph** because it shows each habitat's proportion of the whole.

foundation.question_text:
Monthly nest counts from February to July are recorded.
Which is more appropriate for showing change over time: a line graph or a sector graph?
foundation.solution_text: Use a **line graph** because it shows how the nest count changes over time.

foundation.question_text:
Insect counts at Banksia, Creek and Meadow sites are $14$, $19$ and $11$.
Which is more useful for comparing the counts: a column graph or a sector graph?
foundation.solution_text: Use a **column graph** because column heights make the site counts easy to compare.

development.question_text:
Koala sightings in four reserves are $28$, $46$, $61$ and $73$.
Choose a display for comparing the reserve counts.
development.solution_text: Use a **column graph** to compare the reserve categories.

development.question_text:
A wetland's water level is $35$, $40$, $38$, $47$ and $45$ cm over five consecutive days.
Choose a display for showing change over time.
development.solution_text: Use a **line graph** because the measurements show change over time.

development.question_text:
A park records $16$, $26$, $11$ and $21$ native flowers in four named plots.
Explain why a line graph is not appropriate for comparing the plot counts.
development.solution_text: The named plots are categories. A line joining their counts would suggest meaningful values between plot names.

development.question_text:
A bird survey records species counts of $180$, $240$, $360$ and $420$. A proposed picture graph uses one carefully drawn bird for each sighting.
Explain why a column graph would be more appropriate.
development.solution_text: The picture graph would require many bird drawings and take a long time to draw and read. A **column graph** compares the counts using four columns.

development.question_text:
Rangers record turtle counts in March, April, May, June and July.
What display best shows change over time?
development.solution_text: Use a **line graph** to show how the turtle count changes over time.

development.question_text:
Leaf-litter animals are grouped as ants $34$, beetles $17$, worms $26$ and spiders $9$.
Choose between a column graph and a line graph for comparing the counts.
development.solution_text: Use a **column graph** because the animal groups are categories.

mastery.question_text:
A creek's weekly water-quality score is $62$, $71$, $68$, $79$, $83$ and $77$.
Give one appropriate display for showing change over time and justify your choice.
mastery.solution_text: One appropriate choice is a **line graph** because the score changes over consecutive weeks.

mastery.question_text:
A reserve counts seedlings in habitats A–E: $84$, $37$, $65$, $92$, $48$.
Give one appropriate display for comparing the habitat counts and explain your choice.
mastery.solution_text: One appropriate choice is a **column graph** because the column heights make the habitat counts easy to compare.

mastery.question_text:
A reserve records how many seedlings each of its plots contains: $5$ seedlings in $190$ plots, $6$ in $210$ plots, $7$ in $450$ plots, $8$ in $1050$ plots and $9$ in $880$ plots.
Would a dot plot with one dot per plot be appropriate? Explain why.
mastery.solution_text: No. The data are discrete numerical, but the large frequencies would require too many dots to draw and read easily.
